name: Iris Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a tech and startup lawyer at Quill and Hart, a boutique of about twenty-five lawyers, and my clients are software companies, mostly ten to fifty people. A normal day is a funding round in the morning, which means a stack of investor documents, then software licence contracts in the afternoon and a founder ringing at six asking if they can fire their co-founder. I like founders; they move fast and they say what they think. What wears me out is the redlines, the back-and-forth of tracked changes on the same clause for a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much of that do you do with AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most of the first drafts. I use two AI tools every day, one for drafting and one for comparing versions, and I spend my time on the parts that need judgement. The firm bills a lot of fixed fees, so the faster I am the better our margin. I'm twenty-seven, I live with my partner Dev, who's a product manager at a payments company, and I've got about ten months saved plus a small angel investment in a friend's startup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be surprised. I already see more than 'some routine tasks' at my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was oversold but still worth using, which is a boring, sensible line. Founders would say the same; half of them are selling AI products, so they'd be quieter about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my edge is smaller than I thought but still real. I'm the person at Quill and Hart who turns a term sheet around in a day, and that stays true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools daily, keep billing fixed fees, and push for a bit more share of the margin when I'm reviewed. I'd also keep my angel money where it is and not add more, since a lot of my friend's startup is AI hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your angel investment is in AI hype. What happens to it here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing good. My friend's startup raised money on the word AI, so in a hype-bust world my £5,000 angel cheque is probably a nice lesson. I can afford the lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this quiet world that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev's company, a little. Payments startups raised money on AI stories, and if the stories fade, some of them lay people off. Dev's good, but good people get cut in a funding drought too.

say: AI was **oversold**, but it's still worth using every day on first drafts.
Founders selling **AI products** would go quiet about the hype.
think: My **edge** is smaller than I thought but still real.
I still turn a **term sheet** around in a day.
do: Keep using **two AI tools** daily on drafts and comparisons.
Ask for a bigger share of **fixed-fee margin** at review.
Hold the **angel investment** but add nothing.
S0.quote: My friend's startup raised money on the word AI, so in a hype-bust world my £5,000 angel cheque is probably a nice lesson.
fieldNote: She's **secure** and fast; a plateau just trims her edge.
Her only worry is her partner's **payments startup** in a funding drought.
She treats her **angel money** as a lesson, not a loss she fears.

steps.text: Keep drafting funding documents with two AI tools daily
Ask for a bigger share of fixed-fee margin at the annual review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd plan for. It's basically what my clients are building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to be a lawyer who uses the tools and a hard time for one who doesn't. I'd post about how I run a funding round in half the hours, because founders hire the lawyer who's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. Quill and Hart bills fixed fees, so every hour AI saves is margin, and I'm the one saving it. If anything, I'd ask for a partnership track two years early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first three months I'd build a standard AI workflow for seed rounds and sell it to the partners as a product, a flat fee for small startups. I'd put another £5,000 into an early-stage fund for legal tech. And I'd start a small side business giving workshops to founders on contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. It's my kind of world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's a hard time for lawyers who don't use the tools. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two associates on my floor who still print everything. They're good lawyers. But every hour AI saves at a fixed-fee firm is margin, and I'm the one saving it, so Steady Disruption looks like a promotion to me. For those two, it's a warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Dev see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev's more nervous. Product managers write specs and plan roadmaps, and that's exactly the thinking work on the card. We joke that one of us has to stay employable, and right now I'm winning that joke.

say: It's a **great time** for lawyers who use the tools.
Founders hire the **fast lawyer**, so I'd post how I halve the hours.
think: Every hour AI saves is **margin** at a fixed-fee firm.
I'd push for a **partnership track** two years early.
do: Build a **seed-round workflow** sold as a flat-fee product.
Put **£5,000** into a legal tech fund.
Run paid **contract workshops** for founders on the side.
S1.quote: Every hour AI saves at a fixed-fee firm is margin, and I'm the one saving it, so Steady Disruption looks like a promotion to me.
fieldNote: The change **looks good for her**, so calm is honest, not bravado.
Her household risk sits with **Dev's product job**, which she treats lightly.
She **monetises** the shift three ways: product, fund and workshops.

steps.text: Build an AI seed-round workflow sold as a flat-fee product
Put £5,000 into an early-stage legal tech fund
Run paid contract workshops for startup founders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's not the one I'm ready for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say the winners will be people who own the tools, not people who use them, and I'd mean it as advice. I'd also say regulators need to be fast about liability, because founders will sign whatever the AI drafts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job at Quill and Hart as it exists is gone. Drafting, comparing, advising on standard terms, AGI does all of it, and there's nothing hands-on in my work for the robot delay to protect. Dev's job goes at the same time, so it's both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd leave the firm and co-found a legal AI startup with a developer I know, using about £20,000 of savings. I'd move my angel money into something boring. Dev and I would hold six months' rent as cash, untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but two salaries at risk at the same moment is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why start a company instead of staying at the firm until the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the firm is the thing being replaced. In a two-year AGI world I'd rather be the person selling the robot lawyer than the lawyer it replaces. If it fails, I've lost twenty grand and learned more than in five years of redlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if it didn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat. We rent a nice two-bed in town, and we'd move somewhere half the price within a month. I don't need the balcony to be happy.

say: Winners will **own the tools**, not just use them.
Regulators must move fast on **liability**, because founders sign what AI drafts.
think: My **job as it exists** is gone within two years.
Dev's role goes **at the same time**, so both salaries are at risk.
do: Leave the firm and **co-found** a legal AI startup with about **£20,000**.
Move the **angel money** into something boring.
Hold **six months' rent** as cash with Dev.
feel: **Anxious**, with a plan but two salaries exposed.
S2.quote: In a two-year AGI world I'd rather be the person selling the robot lawyer than the lawyer it replaces.
fieldNote: Both household earners do **desk work**, so the robot delay protects neither.
She moves **first**: leaves the firm to build, true to her adaptability.
She'd cut the **flat** fast, showing realism behind the confidence.

steps.text: Leave Quill and Hart to co-found a legal AI startup
Put about £20,000 of savings into the startup
Hold six months' rent in cash with Dev

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. Enough to build the thing properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about owning the tools, plus that firms should give associates time to build products, not just bill hours. I'd push that at Quill and Hart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have a three-year window to build something on the side while the firm salary pays the rent. After AGI, either the product is the business or I'm job hunting with everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the legal AI tool as a side project in year one, evenings and weekends, with about £10,000. By year three I'd either go full time on it or sell it. I'd keep using every new AI tool at work so I know what's coming before clients do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a good kind, the kind you get before a launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said either the product is the business or you're job hunting. What's the odds, honestly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one in four that it works. Most startups fail, and I've drafted the paperwork for enough of them to know. But the other three outcomes still teach me how the tools work, which is worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for you and Dev?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably decide on kids. I'm twenty-seven, so at thirty-two I'd want to know where I stand first, and the AI timeline would end up deciding it for us, which feels wrong.

say: Firms should give associates time to **build products**, not just bill hours.
The winners will still be people who **own the tools**.
think: I have a **three-year window** to build while the salary pays rent.
After AGI, the **product** is my business or I'm job hunting.
do: Start a **legal AI tool** on the side in year one with £10,000.
Decide by **year three** to go full time or sell.
Use every **new AI tool** at work before clients do.
S3.quote: Most startups fail, and I've drafted the paperwork for enough of them to know.
fieldNote: She's realistic about **startup odds**, from drafting their paperwork.
The **timeline** creeps into family decisions, which she resents.
Income could shrink, but she keeps **control** through the side build.

steps.text: Build a legal AI tool on evenings and weekends in year one
Test every new AI tool at work before clients see it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's almost comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for lawyers to move into new work, and anyone who's still surprised in 2036 wasn't paying attention. That might sound harsh, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thirty-seven, probably with a child, and the end point is the same. The difference is I could make partner, earn well for eight years, and have a business or investments ready before the drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm, aim for partner by thirty-three, and invest steadily, maybe £1,000 a month into a mix including AI companies. I'd learn every tool as it comes. Dev and I would plan a first child around thirty, while both jobs are solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a bit. It's like knowing your lease runs out; you plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd invest in AI companies. Is that betting on your own replacement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that's the point. I'd invest in the AI companies that replace me, because if lawyers are getting replaced, I'd like to own a slice of the replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The partners in their fifties at Quill and Hart who've never touched the tools. They'd be at their peak earnings when AGI lands, and they'd be the ones pretending until the last minute.

say: Ten years is **plenty** for lawyers to move into new work.
Anyone still **surprised in 2036** wasn't paying attention.
think: I could make **partner** and earn well for eight years first.
A **business or investments** must be ready before the drop.
do: Aim for **partner** by thirty-three at Quill and Hart.
Invest about **£1,000 a month**, including AI companies.
Plan a **first child** around thirty with Dev.
feel: Only slightly **uneasy**, like a lease running out.
S4.quote: I'd invest in the AI companies that replace me, because if lawyers are getting replaced, I'd like to own a slice of the replacement.
fieldNote: She treats **ten years** as a runway to build wealth before the drop.
She hedges by **owning** what threatens her job.
Her blunt line about **2036** shows little patience for slow movers.

steps.text: Invest about £1,000 a month, including AI company shares
Learn each new legal AI tool the year it launches
Plan a first child with Dev around age thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Dev and I both do thinking work and we'd be hit in the same year. What would help is clear liability rules so clients still need a human to sign off, and cheap access to the tools, so people like me can build with them instead of just being replaced by them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the people who trained me. The partner who taught me to read a term sheet is fifty-four and has never opened an AI tool, and I don't know what to tell her.

headlineQuote: The partner who taught me to read a term sheet is fifty-four and has never opened an AI tool, and I don't know what to tell her.
portrait: A 27-year-old **tech and startup lawyer** at a boutique firm, drafting funding rounds and software contracts.

She lives with Dev, a **product manager**, with ten months saved and a small angel investment.
Calm through Steady Disruption, she turns **anxious** under fast AGI and plans a legal AI startup.
She wants **liability rules** and believes winners will own the tools, not just use them.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Dev both do thinking work and would be hit together.
